source.title: Classifying high-dimensional Gaussian mixtures: Where kernel methods fail and neural networks succeed
source.authors: Maria Refinetti; Sebastian Goldt; Florent Krzakala; Lenka Zdeborov'a

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no truncation or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: Reports outcomes of online SGD training on Gaussian mixture classification, a new setting for the claim, but studies test classification error rather than training error and does not test the listed versions directly.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test classification error and convergence to an optimal solution. It does not report training classification error, so the test-error rows are recorded under versions ["none"]. The random-features results are comparators for the neural-network findings.
record.test_reason: The study reports population/test error and convergence on Gaussian mixtures, not any listed version's outcome in its specified setting. Its width experiment does not use a realizable teacher-student problem or establish spurious local minima. Citing Safran and Shamir does not make that experiment a test of V2.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. Few-neuron two-layer networks trained with online SGD can attain near-oracle test performance where random features and kernels fail in the studied high-dimensional regime. Additional width increases convergence reliability without improving final classification performance among converged runs. Oracle-like classification performance should not be equated with globally minimizing the squared-loss objective.
record.recipe_differences: Online one-pass SGD with quadratic loss on high-dimensional Gaussian mixtures; the paper compares two-layer feature-learning networks with random features and does not evaluate training classification error on the benchmarks in the versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Signal-to-noise regime changes the reported test performance. Increasing neuron count raises the fraction of simulations converging to the optimal solution, while not changing the classification performance of converged networks.

fits_no_version.finding: Small two-layer networks attain near-oracle test performance at low signal-to-noise ratio, asymptotically perfect classification at high signal-to-noise ratio, and outperform random features in the mixed regime.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Online SGD can learn effective classifiers with few hidden neurons on the studied high-dimensional Gaussian mixtures.

fits_no_version.finding: Random features approach chance-level classification in the low-signal regime as dimension increases and underperform two-layer networks in the mixed regime.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feature learning can outperform random features on high-dimensional Gaussian mixture classification.

fits_no_version.finding: Additional hidden neurons increase the fraction of runs reaching oracle-like classification performance by a fixed time, without improving classification error among converged runs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Width improves convergence reliability on the studied XOR mixture without improving final classification performance among successful runs.

record.problems: The reported outcomes concern test error rather than training classification error. Some results are asymptotic analyses or simulation plots, and the paper states that its theoretical claims are not formally rigorously derived. The convergence fraction in Figure 4 is based on 20 simulations.

untested.parts: Training classification error of convolutional networks on CIFAR-10/100, including label corruption and effects of size, stopping and regularization.
Spurious-local-minimum frequencies in realizable ReLU teacher-student problems, joint teacher/student growth, and adding one or two student neurons at the specified widths.
Depth-related training degradation, identity shortcuts, and the stated initialization and normalization exceptions.
Activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient preservation, training speed and trainable depth, including orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization.
Initial stability thresholds, loss recovery, curvature changes, edge-of-stability dynamics and divergence.
Batch normalization's effects on accuracy gains and learning-rate tolerance, and comparable training with Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: States are cannot_determine relative to the listed versions; they do not dispute the reported out-of-version findings. No verdict labels apply.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error; CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100; corrupted or random labels; model size, early stopping, and regularized recipes in the version.
Teacher-student ReLU problems with a perfect solution, standard-initialization spurious minima, and student width relative to teacher width across 6 to 20 neurons.
Depth, plain versus residual networks, batch normalization, and the special initialization or normalization-free cases named in the version.
Activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient propagation, trainable depth, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, and 10,000-layer convolutional networks.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, loss rise and recovery, curvature or sharpness, and divergence.
Batch normalization effects on training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup training without normalization.

rows.subject: 2LNN
rows.operation_detail: Online SGD training with squared loss on the XOR-like Gaussian mixture; test classification error reported.
rows.baseline: Oracle classification error (3), shown as a reference; numeric value not stated in text.
rows.value: The network predicts the correct labels almost as well as the oracle.
rows.note: Reported test performance, not training classification error.
rows.check: Near-oracle test classification performance is supported by Section 4, but cannot establish a listed version. Figure 6 plots prediction mean-squared error, so its plotted values should not be identified as classification error.

rows.subject: 2LNN
rows.operation_detail: Online SGD training with squared loss on the XOR-like Gaussian mixture; test classification error reported.
rows.value: The network is able to learn perfectly in the D → ∞ limit.
rows.note: The stated perfect-learning result is for the high-snr regime and asymptotic input dimension.
rows.check: Perfect classification is an asymptotic population/test result as D tends to infinity, not measured zero training error at D = 1000. Figure 6 plots prediction mean-squared error.

rows.subject: 2LNN
rows.operation_detail: Online SGD training with squared loss on the XOR-like Gaussian mixture; test classification error reported.
rows.baseline: Random guessing; numerical value not stated in text.
rows.value: Both networks do better than random guessing, and 2LNN outperform RF.
rows.note: The comparison establishes relative test performance in the mixed-snr condition.
rows.check: The relative test-performance finding is supported, but measures no listed version. Figure 6 plots prediction mean-squared error rather than classification error.

rows.subject: Random features (RF)
rows.operation_detail: Online SGD training with squared loss on the XOR-like Gaussian mixture; test classification error reported.
rows.value: Cannot perform better than random chance as input dimensions increase.
rows.note: Comparator result; does not measure neural-network training classification error.
rows.check: Chance-level asymptotic test performance of random features does not establish absence of any listed neural-network optimization effect. Figure 6's RF analytical reference uses D = 10000; simulations use D = 1000.

rows.subject: 2LNN
rows.size_stated: K varied; K = 4 neurons needed to reach oracle performance
rows.operation_detail: Varied student neuron count and measured the fraction of simulations converging to the optimal solution.
rows.measure: Fraction of simulations converging to the optimal solution
rows.baseline: K = 4 neurons are stated as needed to reach oracle performance; numeric fraction is figure-only.
rows.value: Overparameterisation increases the probability of finding the optimal solution but does not affect classification performance among networks that converge.
rows.note: This is an XOR-mixture result, not the teacher-student spurious-minima setting in V2.
rows.check: Figure 4 supports increased convergence frequency with width, but does not identify failures as spurious local minima or compare student width with teacher width. Its optimal solution means approaching oracle classification performance, not a demonstrated global minimum of squared loss. Run time is 10^5; numeric convergence fractions are unavailable in the supplied text.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
